Big Band. A large jazz ensemble format, typically featuring ten to twenty musicians organized into saxophone, trumpet, trombone, and rhythm sections, that dominated American popular music during the Swing Era of the nineteen-thirties and nineteen-forties. The format enabled complex orchestrated arrangements while preserving jazz's improvisational core, allowing soloists to step forward against a disciplined ensemble background. Big band jazz brought jazz from small clubs into concert halls and dance halls, making it America's most popular music.

Big bands typically employ a distinct sectional structure: saxophones, altos and tenors; trumpets; trombones; and a rhythm section of piano, bass, drums, and guitar. Arranged orchestrations allowed composers and arrangers to write complex ensemble passages that featured interlocking horn lines and dynamic shifts. Soloists improvised against the backdrop of ensemble arrangements, creating a dialogue between individual expression and collective discipline. The call-and-response interplay between different horn sections became a defining textural device in big-band swing.

Famous big-band leaders included Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Benny Goodman, Glenn Miller, and Dizzy Gillespie. The Swing Era from 1935 to 1945 saw big-band music become America's primary dance and entertainment music, filling ballrooms and concert halls. By the late nineteen-forties, bebop and smaller jazz combos eclipsed big bands in avant-garde jazz, though the format never entirely disappeared.

Arrangers like Bill Basie, Duke Ellington, and Billy May became celebrities in their own right, recognized for their distinctive orchestration signatures and compositional gifts. Big bands required substantial financial backing and management. The logistics of coordinating fifteen to twenty musicians, travel, and recording made bandleaders as much businessmen as musicians. The recordings and broadcasts of big bands reached millions. Radio airtime was the primary mode of music consumption, and big-band hits became cultural touchstones of the era.

Specific tuning and balance requirements made big-band performance an art. The saxophone section's blend, trumpet brilliance, and trombone foundation required years of ensemble work. The decline of big bands paralleled changes in dance culture and entertainment. Television, smaller jazz clubs, and shifting tastes toward rock and roll drew audiences away. Big band connects to jazz, the Swing Era, Count Basie, Duke Ellington, improvisation, bebop, and the Harlem Renaissance.
